note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. You may use a calculator. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A heating element draws 8 A from a 220 V supply. Using R = V ÷ I, what is its resistance when hot?
A kettle is rated 1800 W at 220 V. Using I = P ÷ V, what current does it draw, to one decimal place?
A 2400 W, 220 V heater is connected to a 110 V supply by mistake. Its resistance stays the same. Using P = V² ÷ R, about what power does it now give?
A 15 Ω resistor is wired in series with a pair of 30 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. What is the total resistance of the network?
Three equal 33 Ω resistors are wired in parallel. What single resistance could replace them?
Ten 100 W lamps are connected in parallel on a 110 V lighting circuit. What total current does the circuit carry?
An air-conditioning unit uses 1.5 kW for 8 hours a day. How many kilowatt-hours (kWh) does it use in a 30-day month?
A 3 kW water heater runs for 2 hours a day for 30 days. Energy costs J$60 per kWh (an example rate). What is the cost of running it for the month?
A single-phase motor takes 10 A from a 220 V supply at a power factor of 0.8. Using P = V × I × power factor, what is its real power?
A single-phase load takes 15 A from a 220 V supply. What is its apparent power (V × I)?
Why does a low power factor matter when you size the cable for a motor circuit?
options: It lowers the current, so a smaller cable can be used
It raises the current for the same real power
It changes the frequency of the supply
It changes the speed of the motor but not the current

questions.stem: A bell transformer's windings have 1100 turns (primary) and 60 turns (secondary). With 220 V on the primary, what voltage does the secondary give?
A 220 V / 12 V transformer supplies 5 A at 12 V. Ignoring losses, about what current does it take from the 220 V supply?
A borehole pump's motor gives 2.0 kW of shaft power while drawing 2.5 kW of electrical power. How efficient is it?
An imported motor nameplate says 3 hp. Taking 1 hp as 746 W, about what is its output in kilowatts?
The synchronous speed of a motor is n = 120 × f ÷ p, where f is the frequency and p is the number of poles. What is the synchronous speed of a 4-pole motor on Jamaica's 50 Hz supply?
A motor with a synchronous speed of 1500 rev/min runs at 1440 rev/min on full load. What is its slip, as a percentage of the synchronous speed?
Using R = ρ × L ÷ A, with ρ for copper as 0.0172 Ω·mm²/m, what is the resistance of one 50 m length of 2.5 mm² copper conductor?
The two conductors of a circuit together have a resistance of 0.4 Ω, and the load current is 20 A. What percentage of a 220 V supply is lost as voltage drop?
A circuit is re-run in the same cable size, with the same load, but the run is now twice as long. What happens to the voltage drop?
options: It becomes four times as large

questions.stem: A cable table gives a voltage drop of 18 mV per amp per metre (mV/A/m). The load is 16 A and the run is 25 m. What is the voltage drop?
A specification limits voltage drop to 3% of a 220 V supply. Which calculated drop meets the limit?
A circuit's design current is 17 A and its cable is rated 27 A as installed. Breakers come in 10, 16, 20 and 32 A. Which breaker is the right choice?
Why must a circuit breaker's rating be no higher than the current rating of the cable it protects?
options: So that the breaker trips each time the load starts
So that the load receives a higher voltage
So that the cable is protected from overheating
So that the earth fault current is made smaller

questions.stem: A cable is rated 32 A on its own. When grouped with other cables, its rating must be multiplied by 0.7. What is its rating when grouped?
A cable rated 40 A runs through a hot roof space (factor 0.87) and is grouped with others (factor 0.8). Applying both factors, about what is its rating?
A conduit has an inside area of 314 mm². The rule for this job is that cables may fill no more than 40% of it. What total cable area may be drawn in?
A cable has an overall diameter of 10 mm. Using A = π × d² ÷ 4 and π = 3.142, what is the area it takes up?
A cable tray climbs 1.5 m over a level distance of 2.0 m. How long is the sloping section of tray?
A conduit offset made with two 30° bends needs the bends spaced at 2 × the offset depth. The conduit must step out 75 mm to clear a beam. How far apart are the two bends?
A 6 m ladder leans against a wall at 75° to the ground. How high up the wall does it reach? (sin 75° = 0.966)
A room 5 m × 4 m needs an average of 300 lux (lumens per square metre). Ignoring losses, how many lumens must reach the working surface?
Number of fittings N = (E × A) ÷ (F × UF × MF). An office of 50 m² needs E = 400 lux. Each fitting gives F = 3600 lm, with UF = 0.5 and MF = 0.8. How many fittings are needed?
A lighting calculation shows that 13.2 fittings are needed for a room. How many should be planned?
options: 14, rounding up so the light level is reached
13, rounding to the nearest whole number

questions.stem: A small shop has lighting of 800 W, socket loads of 2400 W and a 1500 W air conditioner. What is the total connected load?
Socket loads in an office add up to 6000 W. The designer expects only 40% of this to be in use at one time. What demand should be allowed for the sockets?
A job needs 185 m of cable. You allow 10% extra for waste and terminations, and the cable comes in 100 m rolls. How many rolls should be ordered?
Materials cost the firm J$45 000, and it marks them up by 20%. What does it charge the client for them, before GCT?
A quotation for wiring a house must show GCT. How should the GCT be worked out?
options: At the current rate, on the price before tax
On the cost before mark-up, at a rate the client agrees
Not at all, because labour is never taxed
As a fixed J$ amount added to each line

questions.stem: A team of 3 electricians wires 12 points a day. At the same rate, how many days will the same team need to wire 54 points?
Five insulation resistance readings are 120, 150, 180, 110 and 140 MΩ. What is their mean (average)?
A voltmeter reads 214 V when connected to a calibrator set at 220 V. What is the meter's percentage error?
On Jamaica's 50 Hz supply, how long does one complete cycle last? (Period = 1 ÷ frequency.)
On a 1:50 floor plan, a cable route measures 84 mm. How long is the real route?
A trainee's sheet shows that a 1 kW, 220 V heater draws 45 A. What is the best next step?
options: Order cable rated for 45 A for the heater circuit
Fit a 50 A breaker to be on the safe side
Check the working, since a rough estimate gives about 4.5 A
Ask the client to buy a smaller heater

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show your working. You may use a calculator. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What name is given to the ratio of real power (kW) to apparent power (kVA)?
A 220 V circuit supplies a 4.4 kW heating load. What current flows, in amperes?
A lamp draws 0.5 A from a 110 V supply. What is its resistance when lit, in ohms?
A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are wired in parallel. What is their combined resistance, in ohms?
A transformer for 24 V door-entry equipment is fed at 220 V, and its primary winding has 1100 turns. Work out the number of secondary turns.
What is the synchronous speed, in rev/min, of a 2-pole motor on a 50 Hz supply?
A 2 kW heater runs for 90 minutes. How many kilowatt-hours of energy does it use?
A shop uses 450 kWh in a month. Energy costs J$55 per kWh (an example rate). What is the cost, in J$?
Real power is measured in watts. In what unit is apparent power measured?
A cable data sheet gives 7.41 mΩ/m for one conductor. Find the resistance of a 40 m run of that conductor, in ohms, to two decimal places.
A circuit on a 220 V supply has a voltage drop of 5.5 V. What is this as a percentage of the supply voltage?
Output 3.7 kW, input 4.6 kW: work out this motor's efficiency to the nearest whole percent.
What name is given to a number less than 1 by which a cable's current rating is multiplied when it is grouped with others or run in a hot place?
Three earth continuity readings are 0.42 Ω, 0.38 Ω and 0.40 Ω. What is their mean, in ohms?
A load is rated 10 kVA and runs at a power factor of 0.85. What is its real power, in kW?

essays.stem: A 3 kW, 220 V water heater is to have its own circuit. Explain how you would work out its design current, choose the circuit breaker and check the cable size. Show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the design current: I = P ÷ V = 3000 ÷ 220 = about 13.6 A. The breaker must be equal to or bigger than this, so from the usual sizes (10, 16, 20 A) I choose 16 A. The cable must then carry at least the breaker rating after any rating factors. I look at the maker's cable table for the way the cable is installed, for example in conduit on a wall. If the roof space is hot or the cable is grouped, I multiply the table rating by the factors; for example a cable rated 27 A × 0.87 = 23.5 A, which is still above 16 A, so it is suitable. The rule is: design current ≤ breaker rating ≤ cable rating as installed. Last, I check the voltage drop for the length of the run against the limit in the specification. I record each step so the supervisor can check it.
markingPoints: Design current worked out correctly: 3000 ÷ 220 ≈ 13.6 A
Breaker chosen at or above the design current (16 A)
Cable rating taken from the maker's table for the installation method
Rating factors (heat, grouping) applied and checked against the breaker: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz
Voltage drop checked and the working recorded

essays.stem: A 220 V radial circuit 25 m long feeds an outbuilding with a load of 18 A. The cable table gives 18 mV/A/m for 2.5 mm² cable and 11 mV/A/m for 4 mm² cable. The specification allows a 3% voltage drop. Work out which cable size is acceptable, and explain your answer.
essays.modelAnswer: The allowed drop is 3% of 220 V = 0.03 × 220 = 6.6 V. Voltage drop = mV/A/m × current × length ÷ 1000. For 2.5 mm² cable: 18 × 18 × 25 = 8100 mV = 8.1 V. This is more than 6.6 V (about 3.7%), so 2.5 mm² is not acceptable, even if it could carry the current. For 4 mm² cable: 11 × 18 × 25 = 4950 mV = about 4.95 V, which is about 2.25% and below 6.6 V, so 4 mm² is acceptable. I would also check that the 4 mm² cable's current rating, after any rating factors, is above the breaker rating. The longer the run, the more the drop matters, so long runs often need a bigger cable than the current alone would suggest. Too much drop makes motors run hot and lamps dim.
markingPoints: Allowed drop worked out: 6.6 V
2.5 mm² drop worked out (8.1 V) and rejected
4 mm² drop worked out (about 4.95 V) and accepted
Units handled correctly (mV converted to V)
Explains why drop matters on long runs or what too much drop does

essays.stem: Explain what power factor is, using a motor that takes 12 A from a 220 V supply at a power factor of 0.75 as a worked example. Say why power factor matters to an electrician.
essays.modelAnswer: Power factor is the ratio of real power, which does useful work and is measured in watts, to apparent power, which is volts × amps and is measured in volt-amperes. Motors, fluorescent ballasts and transformers have coils, so their current is out of step with the voltage and the power factor is below 1. For the motor: apparent power = 220 × 12 = 2640 VA. Real power = 2640 × 0.75 = 1980 W. So the motor takes 12 A, but only 1980 W does work. If the power factor were 1, the same 1980 W would need only 1980 ÷ 220 = 9 A. This matters because the cable, breaker and switchgear must carry the full 12 A, not the current worked out from watts alone. A low power factor also means more losses in cables and can bring charges from the power company for large users. It can be improved with capacitors, chosen by a designer.
markingPoints: Defines power factor as real power ÷ apparent power (W ÷ VA)
Apparent power worked out: 2640 VA
Real power worked out: 1980 W
Explains that cables and protection must carry the actual current
Mentions losses or correction with capacitors

essays.stem: A classroom 8 m × 6 m needs an average of 300 lux. Each fitting gives 4000 lumens, the utilisation factor is 0.6 and the maintenance factor is 0.8. Work out how many fittings are needed, and explain each step and how you would lay them out.
essays.modelAnswer: The area is 8 × 6 = 48 m². The lumens needed on the desks are E × A = 300 × 48 = 14 400 lm. Not all the light from a fitting reaches the desks: the utilisation factor (0.6) allows for light lost on walls and ceiling, and the maintenance factor (0.8) allows for dirt and lamps getting dimmer with age. So each fitting gives 4000 × 0.6 × 0.8 = 1920 useful lumens. N = 14 400 ÷ 1920 = 7.5, so I round up to 8 fittings, because rounding down would leave the room below 300 lux. I would lay them out as 2 rows of 4, spaced evenly, with the space between fittings about twice the space from the end fittings to the wall, so the light is even. I would check the maker's spacing limit and record the calculation on the lighting layout.
markingPoints: Area and total lumens worked out (48 m², 14 400 lm)
Explains UF and MF and finds useful lumens per fitting (1920 lm)
N = 7.5, rounded up to 8, with the reason
Sensible even layout (for example 2 rows of 4)
Mentions checking spacing or recording the result

essays.stem: A small shop in Ocho Rios has lighting of 0.6 kW used 12 hours a day, an air conditioner of 1.8 kW used 10 hours a day, and a fridge that uses 0.2 kW on average for 24 hours. Energy costs J$60 per kWh (an example rate). Work out the monthly cost for 30 days, show your working, and suggest two ways to cut it.
essays.modelAnswer: Energy in kWh = kW × hours. Lighting: 0.6 × 12 = 7.2 kWh a day. Air conditioner: 1.8 × 10 = 18 kWh a day. Fridge: 0.2 × 24 = 4.8 kWh a day. Total = 7.2 + 18 + 4.8 = 30 kWh a day. For 30 days: 30 × 30 = 900 kWh. Cost = 900 × 60 = J$54 000 for the month. The air conditioner uses the most, about 60% of the energy, so savings there matter most: set the thermostat a little higher, keep doors closed and service the filters, or replace it with an inverter unit. The lighting could be changed to LED fittings, which give the same light for much less power, and switched off when the shop is closed. I would show the owner the working in a table so they can see where the money goes, and note that the real rate comes from their bill.
markingPoints: Daily kWh for each load worked out correctly
Daily total (30 kWh) and monthly total (900 kWh)
Monthly cost worked out: J$54 000
Identifies the largest user (air conditioner)
Two sensible savings suggested (thermostat, LEDs, switching off, servicing)

essays.stem: Describe the steps for working out the cable needed for three lighting circuits that each follow a 70 m route, and pricing it for a quotation. Each circuit needs a line, a neutral and an earth conductor. Show a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: First I measure each route from the drawing using its scale, or on site, and add drops to switches and fittings. Here each route is 70 m. Each circuit needs three conductors, so one circuit needs 3 × 70 = 210 m of single conductor, and three circuits need 3 × 210 = 630 m. I add an allowance for waste and terminations, say 10%: 630 × 1.1 = 693 m. The conductor comes in 100 m rolls, so I order 7 rolls, and I split them by colour as the circuits need. Next I multiply the rolls by the supplier's price, add the other materials (conduit, boxes, fixings), and add the firm's mark-up. Finally I add GCT at the current rate on the total before tax. I write down every step and check the totals with a quick estimate, so another person can follow and check my quote.
markingPoints: Measures routes from the scaled drawing or on site
Multiplies by the number of conductors and circuits (630 m)
Adds a waste allowance and rounds up to whole rolls (7 rolls)
Prices materials and adds mark-up, then GCT at the current rate
Records and checks the working

essays.stem: A 12 V DC supply feeds a 4 Ω resistor in series with two 12 Ω resistors that are in parallel with each other. Work out the total resistance, the supply current, the voltage across each part and the current in each 12 Ω resistor. Say how you would check your answers with a meter.
essays.modelAnswer: The two 12 Ω resistors in parallel give 12 × 12 ÷ (12 + 12) = 6 Ω. This is in series with 4 Ω, so the total is 4 + 6 = 10 Ω. The supply current is I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 A. The voltage across the 4 Ω resistor is 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 V, and across the parallel pair it is 1.2 × 6 = 7.2 V. The two add up to 12 V, which checks. Each 12 Ω resistor has 7.2 V across it, so each carries 7.2 ÷ 12 = 0.6 A, and 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2 A, which matches the supply current. To check with a meter, I first measure the total resistance with the supply off. Then, on this low-voltage bench supply only, I measure the voltage across each part with the meter in parallel, and the current with the meter in series. I compare the readings with my answers and allow for the resistor tolerance.
markingPoints: Parallel pair = 6 Ω and total = 10 Ω
Supply current = 1.2 A
Voltages 4.8 V and 7.2 V, checked to add to 12 V
Branch currents 0.6 A each
Describes meter checks: resistance with supply off, voltmeter in parallel, ammeter in series

essays.stem: A 4-pole motor has a nameplate that shows 50 Hz, 1450 rev/min, 5.5 kW output and 6.4 kW input at full load. Work out its synchronous speed, its slip and its efficiency, and explain why the nameplate frequency must match the supply.
essays.modelAnswer: Synchronous speed n = 120 × f ÷ p = 120 × 50 ÷ 4 = 1500 rev/min. This is the speed of the rotating magnetic field. The rotor runs a little slower, at 1450 rev/min, so the slip is (1500 − 1450) ÷ 1500 × 100 = about 3.3%. Efficiency = output ÷ input × 100 = 5.5 ÷ 6.4 × 100 = about 86%. The rest, about 0.9 kW, is lost as heat and friction. The nameplate frequency must match the supply because the speed depends on the frequency. A motor made for a different frequency would run at the wrong speed in Jamaica, and its current and heating could be wrong, so the pump or fan it drives would not give its rated output and the motor could overheat. I would always check the frequency and voltage on the nameplate before the motor is installed.
markingPoints: Synchronous speed worked out: 1500 rev/min
Slip worked out: about 3.3%
Efficiency worked out: about 86%
Explains that speed depends on frequency
Explains the effect of a mismatch (wrong speed, overheating) and checking the nameplate

essays.stem: A control panel uses a 100 VA transformer, 220 V to 24 V. Work out the full-load secondary current and the primary current, ignoring losses, and explain how these figures help you choose its protection.
essays.modelAnswer: A transformer's VA rating is the same on both sides if losses are ignored. Secondary current = VA ÷ V = 100 ÷ 24 = about 4.2 A. Primary current = 100 ÷ 220 = about 0.45 A. The voltage is stepped down by about 9 times, so the current is stepped up by about the same amount. These figures tell me the most current each winding should carry. The secondary protection must be no larger than the secondary rating, so a fuse or breaker of about 4 A protects the winding and the control wiring from overload. The primary protection is chosen from the maker's data, because a transformer takes a short surge of current when it is switched on, so a fuse that is too small may blow at switch-on. I would check the maker's table, record the figures, and make sure the control wiring is sized for the secondary current.
markingPoints: Secondary current worked out: about 4.2 A
Primary current worked out: about 0.45 A
Explains the turns ratio: voltage down, current up
Secondary protection no larger than the secondary rating
Primary protection from maker's data, allowing for switch-on surge

essays.stem: As a Level 3 team member you check a trainee's calculation sheet for a new circuit before materials are ordered. Describe what you look for and how you check it, and give an example of a common mistake you might find.
essays.modelAnswer: First I check that the sheet says what the job is, which drawing and tables were used, and the date and the trainee's name. I check the input figures: the load in watts, the supply voltage (110 V or 220 V), the route length and the installation method. Then I check each step is written out with units, so I can follow it. I redo the key steps myself or work them backwards, for example multiplying the current by the voltage to get back to the power. I also do a rough estimate: a 2 kW load on 220 V should be about 9 A, so an answer of 90 A is clearly wrong. A common mistake is mixing units, such as using millivolts as volts in a voltage-drop sum, or kW as W. Another is forgetting to apply rating factors. I talk the trainee through any mistakes, have them correct the sheet, and sign it as checked.
markingPoints: Checks the input data and sources (load, voltage, length, tables)
Checks working is set out step by step with units
Rechecks by redoing, working backwards or estimating
Gives a realistic common mistake (units, missing factors, wrong voltage)
Has the trainee correct it and signs or records the check

practical1.title: Calculate, build and measure resistor networks on a 12 V DC bench supply
practical1.brief: As a group, work out and then prove by measurement the resistance, current and voltage in four resistor networks set by the assessor (series, parallel and two series–parallel networks). The supply is a 12 V DC bench power supply only; no mains circuit is used. Each member is given one network: they calculate the total resistance, the supply current, and the voltage and current in each resistor on the group's calculation sheet, then build their network on the breadboard or terminal board. With the supply off, they measure the total resistance; with the 12 V supply on, they measure the voltages (meter in parallel) and the supply current (meter in series). Each member works out the percentage difference between the calculated and measured values and explains any difference. Another member checks each calculation and signs it. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: 12 V DC bench power supply with current limit
Resistors (for example 10 Ω, 22 Ω, 47 Ω, 100 Ω, 2 × 12 Ω, 2 × 100 Ω), rated for the power in each network
Breadboard or terminal board and jumper leads
Group calculation sheet and result table from the assessor
photos: The calculation sheet for each network before building
Each network built on the board, with the supply off
The meter measuring total resistance with the supply off
The meter measuring a voltage across one resistor with the supply on
The meter connected in series measuring the supply current
The finished result table, with calculated and measured values and percentage differences
checklist: Calculated total resistance, current and voltages correctly, showing the working and units
Built the network to match the diagram
Measured resistance only with the supply off
Connected the meter correctly: in parallel for voltage, in series for current, on the right range
Worked out the percentage difference and gave a sensible reason for it (resistor tolerance, meter accuracy)
Checked another member's calculation and signed it
Switched off the supply before changing the circuit and left the bench tidy
safety: Use only the 12 V DC bench supply; no mains circuit is built
Set the supply's current limit before switching on, and switch off before changing any connection
Resistors can get hot: do not touch them while the supply is on
Keep drinks away from the bench and report any damaged leads

practical2.title: Load schedule, cable sizing and voltage-drop check for a small building, with a priced cable list
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out the calculations for wiring a small building from the drawing and data sheet given by the assessor (for example a two-bedroom house or a shop). First, measure two real cable routes in the Centre's workshop with a tape (for example from the training distribution board to two outlets) and record them. Then share out the circuits so that every member does at least one: work out its design current (110 V or 220 V as the drawing shows), choose the breaker, take the cable rating from the table, apply the rating factors given, and check the voltage drop against the 3% limit in the specification. Together, build the load schedule, work out the total connected load and the demand, and prepare a cable take-off with a waste allowance and a priced list using the price list given (add mark-up as the assessor says, and GCT at the current rate the assessor gives). Each member's calculations are checked and signed by another member. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Drawing of a small building with loads marked, and a specification from the assessor
Cable rating and voltage-drop table, rating factors and a price list from the assessor
Tape measure (at least 10 m) and a scale rule
Blank load schedule and take-off sheets
photos: The tape measure laid along each real route in the workshop, with the length recorded
The drawing with the routes marked and measured to scale
A completed circuit calculation sheet for each member
The finished load schedule with totals and demand
The cable take-off and priced list
The sheets signed as checked by another member
checklist: Measured the real routes accurately and recorded them
Worked out the design current for their circuit correctly for its voltage
Chose a breaker and a cable that meet design current ≤ breaker ≤ cable rating after rating factors
Worked out the voltage drop and compared it with the 3% limit, choosing a bigger cable if needed
Added a waste allowance and rounded up to whole rolls or lengths
Priced the list correctly, with mark-up and GCT added in the right order
Checked another member's work and signed it
safety: Do not open any distribution board or enclosure to measure routes; measure along the outside only
Keep walkways clear when laying out the tape, and watch for trip hazards
Do not climb on equipment to measure; use a stepladder checked by the assessor, with a second person holding it
